newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's provinces to meet on national unity issue.
newsitem.headline: Canada's provinces to meet on national unity issue.

text.p: The leaders of Canada's nine English-speaking provinces said on Friday they will hold an informal meeting to discuss the hotly-debated issue of Canada's national unity, without the participation of French-speaking Quebec.

The announcement, made jointly by the provincial premiers at the end of a two-day gathering in this Atlantic seaside resort, made no reference to any participation in the coming national unity meeting by Canada's federal government.

Quebec separatist Premier Lucien Bouchard, who threatened to walk out of this week's meeting if national unity was discussed, said he had accepted the decision of the other provinces to tackle the question, but Quebec had opted not take part.
"I know that I would be welcome at this meeting. But I also know that this meeting would function more efficiently toward its real goals in my absence," Bouchard told a news conference.
In reference to the national unity question, Bouchard said: "Basically everything has been said. The consultation process will lead nowhere, but I'm just not going to get involved."
One of the veterans of the national unity debate in Canada spoke of the planned meeting as a first step in mobilizing Canada's downhearted federalist forces.

"I'm happy about this decision by the premiers because we will end what I have feared is a sleepwalk into the inevitability of the next Quebec election and what might flow from the next Quebec election," said Saskatchewan Premier Roy Romanow.

Quebec's secessionists were defeated by a razor thin margin in a sovereignty refendum in October 1995. It was the second time in 15 years that the separatist forces had been rebuffed in a Quebec referendum.
Quebec is expected to hold a provincial election sometime in 1998, which is widely expected to be a precursor to another referendum on whether Quebec should break away from the rest of Canada.
